questions.q: The wine town of Langenlois gives its wine to a DAC named after the Danube tributary that flows past it. Which river is that?
questions.exp: Langenlois is the heart of the Kamptal, the valley of the Kamp, which the Court prints as the Kampt River; its DAC is for dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, with the Heiligenstein above Zöbing as its great site. The Krems gives its name to the neighbouring Kremstal and the Traisen to the Traisental, both also tributaries of the Danube.

questions.q: Knoll and Prager, two of the producers the Court names, both make their wine in which Austrian DAC?
questions.exp: Knoll at Unterloiben and Prager at Weissenkirchen farm the terraces of the Wachau gorge, and Prager was among the founders of the Vinea Wachau in 1983, whose Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd both houses use. Of the Court's other names, Bründlmayer and Schloss Gobelsburg are in the Kamptal, while the two Pichler estates are also Wachau houses.

questions.q: Schloss Gobelsburg, a Cistercian castle estate among the Court's named producers, lies in which DAC?
questions.exp: Schloss Gobelsburg sits at the southern end of the Kamptal near Langenlois, with holdings in the Heiligenstein and the Lamm, and keeps a tradition line made in old wooden casks. Bründlmayer, also on the Court's list, is the Kamptal's other benchmark house, so two of the Court's six Austrian names belong to this one valley.

questions.q: The Court names two hard-to-pair vegetables that Grüner Veltliner handles well. Name either one.
questions.exp: Asparagus and artichokes make most wines taste metallic or oddly sweet, but an unoaked, crisp, dry Grüner Veltliner with its green, peppery edge meets them on their own terms. The Court also pairs it with fresh seafood, smoked fish, herby dishes, fresh cheeses and schnitzel, all of which suit its purity and acidity.

questions.q: What name does the Court give the Austrian wine capsule that marks a wine of Qualitätswein level or higher?
questions.exp: The banderole is the red-white-red strip across the capsule of every Austrian Qualitätswein, Prädikatswein included, and it carries the state test number. Wein and Landwein never wear it. The Prüfnummer is the number itself, Goldkapsel is a German producer's mark for a richer selection, and Weinsiegel is a German quality seal.

questions.q: Which Wachau category, the middle of the three by ripeness, takes its name from a tool used in falconry?
questions.exp: The Vinea Wachau's three categories run Steinfeder, named for a feathery grass, then Federspiel, named for the lure a falconer swings to call the bird back, then Smaragd, named for the emerald lizards on the terrace walls. Federspiel is the dry, medium-bodied wine for the table, between the light Steinfeder and the rich Smaragd.

questions.q: Zweigelt, one of the Court's two Austrian reds, was bred in 1922 by crossing Blaufränkisch with which grape?
questions.exp: Zweigelt was bred at Klosterneuburg in 1922 from Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent and is now Austria's most planted red: sour cherry, soft tannin, juicy and easy to chill. Blaufränkisch, the old parent, is the deeper, peppery grape of Mittelburgenland, while Blauburger is a different crossing, of Blauer Portugieser with Blaufränkisch.

questions.q: Which kind of oak does the Court say is rarely used in making Austrian white wine?
questions.exp: Austrian whites are made for purity of fruit, fermented in stainless steel or large old casks that give texture without an oak flavour, and the Court notes that new oak is rarely used for them. The aim is the crisp, unoaked Grüner Veltliner and Riesling of the Danube, very dry or, in Burgenland, very sweet.
